query: More than a century of research on conventional steels and other alloys has shown that exposure within certain temperature ranges can sharply reduce toughness and threaten safety in aerospace, shipping, and petrochemical applications. High-entropy alloys offer attractive strength, ductility, resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement, and wear resistance; however, their multicomponent chemistry complicates predictions of long-term mechanical reliability. Their resistance to rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation does not establish whether their toughness will remain stable after service-relevant heating, and this uncertainty limits engineering use. For a high-performance multicomponent high-entropy alloy in its as-designed condition, under the constraint that its original strength–ductility combination must be retained, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to reduce post-exposure toughness degradation? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to an otherwise identical untreated baseline, define the temperature, duration, and loading boundaries, identify supporting evidence from the observations summarized above, and describe a decisive experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a specific alloying element, such as aluminum or titanium, to a high-entropy alloy can reduce post-exposure toughness degradation by forming a stable solid solution structure and minimizing the formation of deleterious intermetallic phases.
generation.material_initial_state: As-designed high-entropy alloy with a multicomponent chemistry
generation.intervention: Addition of a specific alloying element, such as aluminum or titanium
generation.conditions: Service-relevant heating, with temperature ranges between 600°C to 1000°C, and duration of several hours
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable solid solution structure and minimization of deleterious intermetallic phases
generation.mechanism: The added alloying element enhances the solid solution strengthening effect, reduces lattice distortion, and inhibits the formation of brittle phases, thereby improving the alloy's toughness and resistance to degradation
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced post-exposure toughness degradation, with a retained strength-ductility combination, compared to an otherwise identical untreated baseline
generation.baseline: Untreated high-entropy alloy with the same composition and processing history
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 600°C to 1000°C, duration: several hours, loading conditions: tensile or compressive loading
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the alloying element's effect on the alloy's microstructure and properties is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of the microstructure, mechanical properties, and toughness of the high-entropy alloy with and without the added alloying element, after exposure to service-relevant heating conditions
measurements: Microstructural analysis using TEM or SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the added alloying element does not result in a significant reduction in post-exposure toughness degradation, or if the alloy's microstructure and properties are not significantly improved, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: High entropy alloys consist of alloying elements with five or more equal molar fractions, each of which has a molar fraction of about 5% to 35%. As a kind of comprehensive material, high entropy alloy has better physical and chemical properties than many common metal compounds []. Therefore, it has attracted wide attention in material science and engineering and is the focus field of scholars at home and abroad [,]. In recent years, many scholars at home and abroad have used high entropy alloys for surface modification, mainly by laser melting, laser deposition, and plasma melting. The lower preparation cost and excellent performance of high entropy alloys not only improve their service life and significantly reduce the failure loss but also reduce their surface repair cost, and high entropy alloys have many advantages that traditional alloys can hardly match []. However, there are difficulties in the synergistic enhancement of strength, toughness, and corrosion resistance of high entropy alloys, and no satisfactory solution has been found so far []. The equiatomic Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy is one of the most attractive RHEAs, which solidifies as a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) microstructure with heterogeneous elemental distribution and exhibits excellent high-temperature strength and room-temperature ductility (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta has an extremely high compressive yield strength, 1273 MPa at room temperature and 688 MPa at 900°C (). By comparison, conventional high-temperature Ni-base superalloys notably soften above 600°C, with the compressive yield strength dropping to ~200 MPa at 900°C (). Equimolar Ti-V-Nb-Ta also exhibits impressive tensile ductility, ~14% at room temperature (), and a relatively low brittle-to-ductile transition temperature between −47° and −27°C, comparable to BCC metals and stainless steels for engineering applications (, ). AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) have drawn significant attention due to their unique design and superior mechanical properties. Comprising 5–35 at% of five or more elements with similar atomic radii, HEAs exhibit high configurational entropy, resulting in single-phase solid solutions rather than intermetallic compounds. Additive manufacturing (AM), particularly direct energy deposition (DED), is effective for producing HEAs due to its rapid cooling rates, which ensure uniform microstructures and minimize defects. These alloys typically form face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) structures, contributing to their exceptional strength, hardness, and mechanical performance across various temperatures. However, FCC-structured HEAs often have low yield strengths, posing a challenge for structural applications. In this study, a Ni-Co-Fe-Cr-Al-Ti HEA was manufactured using the DED method. This study proposes that the addition of aluminum and titanium creates a γ + γ′ phase structure within a multicomponent FCC-HEA matrix, enhancing the thermal stability and coarsening the resistance and strength. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) constitute one of the most innovative classes of metallic materials, attracting significant attention from both scientific and industrial communities in recent years [,,]. Their uniqueness lies in the design of chemical composition, where several principal elements are present in nearly equimolar proportions, leading to the formation of high-entropy phases with simplified crystalline structures [,]. These materials exhibit exceptional mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties, often surpassing those of traditional engineering alloys [,]. HEAs, particularly the Cantor alloy (CoCrFeMnNi), remain among the most recognized and extensively studied representatives within this group []. Since its discovery, the Cantor alloy has attracted significant scientific attention due to its exceptional mechanical properties, distinguishing it from both conventional and other HEAs [,]. It exhibits a single-phase FCC structure with excellent ductility and resistance to brittle fracture, even under cryogenic conditions [,,].
